extracted.intended_audience: Congressional staff, policymakers, regulatory agency officials, and policy analysts concerned with U.S. federal regulatory process
extracted.subtask_description: A policy-primer style set of standards and concrete recommendations for improving the U.S. federal regulatory process across stages: congressional authorization, agency rulewriting, judicial review, retrospective analysis, and congressional oversight. Focuses on instituting evidence-based analysis, prospective and retrospective impact accounting, and institutional changes to improve regulatory quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations should solve real problems at an acceptable cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations should solve real problems at an acceptable cost; regulators must carefully and completely disclose the likely effects of individual rules and of the regulatory system as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisionmakers should not proceed 'in ignorance of the tradeoffs'—regulatory action requires demonstrating that the regulation will effectively solve the intended problem and that the benefits justify the costs (consistent with Executive Order 12866, while allowing nondomesticated values to be considered).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-based assessment of the problem (existence, size, cause)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should conduct an evidence-based assessment of the underlying problem: demonstrate the existence, extent, and cause of the problem a regulation seeks to solve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The primer documents many examples where agencies failed to provide evidence the rule would solve the problem (e.g., SEC accredited investor change; FDA animal feed rule). Regulatory impact analyses should assess the problem using best available evidence rather than anecdote or presumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop and evaluate a limited range of alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should identify a small number or limited range of reasonable alternatives to regulation and analyze them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatives may include nonregulatory approaches (education, voluntary measures), narrower scopes (e.g., apply rule only to pet food not all animal feed), or metrics-based standards (actuarial equivalence). Failure to consider credible alternatives leads to unnecessary costs and missed solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess and, where feasible, monetize benefits and costs for significant rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory analyses should estimate the benefits and costs of alternatives, including monetized estimates for economically significant rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executive Order 12866 requires agencies to consider benefits and costs for economically significant rules (commonly defined as > $100 million annually). The primer notes that only a small fraction of rules had monetized benefit and cost estimates and recommends statutory requirements to improve this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require regulatory impact analysis (RIA) for economically significant rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutorily require all agencies to conduct regulatory impact analysis for regulations with economic effects exceeding a certain threshold (e.g., $100 million/year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute should indicate the topics RIA must cover: assessment of the existence, extent, and cause of the problem; development of alternatives; and assessment of the benefits and costs of alternatives. This should apply to independent agencies as well as executive agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish preliminary analysis for public comment before selecting preferred approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should publish their preliminary analysis of the problem and the benefits and costs of each alternative for public comment before selecting a preferred approach and writing a regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This promotes public participation and better-informed decisionmaking by exposing assumptions and alternatives early in the process rather than using analysis post-hoc to justify decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational independence and career incentives for analysts
rubrics_metrics.description: Place economists and other analysts in units separate from the program office that writes regulations and manage them by other analysts with clear career criteria tied to quality and objectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free analysts to conduct objective analysis; have analysts report to and be managed by other analysts, with career advancement based on analytical quality rather than program office priorities to reduce political or programmatic pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve agencies' prospective information about likely effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Before issuing economically significant regulations, agencies must understand the nature and cause of the problem, develop alternatives, and assess benefits and costs of each alternative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This restates Executive Order 12866 requirements and argues for stronger statutory backing and better enforcement (including for independent agencies) because EO requirements can be ignored when other presidential priorities prevail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify courts' role in reviewing agency economic analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress should specify by statute the topics a regulatory impact analysis must cover and clarify how courts are expected to review agencies’ economic analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend three legislative changes: (1) specify by statute the RIA topics (problem, alternatives, benefits, costs); (2) require agencies to base RIAs on the best available evidence; (3) make the agency's RIA part of the rulemaking record and reviewable by courts only if a deficiency materially affected the decision—this aims to ensure courts scrutinize significant analytical deficiencies while avoiding trivial remands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make RIA/relevant economic analysis part of the rulemaking record
rubrics_metrics.description: Require agencies to include regulatory impact analysis or other economic analysis as part of the rulemaking record so it is reviewable by courts under specified conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make analysis reviewable only when a deficiency made a material difference in the regulatory decision; this helps judicial review focus on meaningful analytic flaws rather than trivialities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutionalize retrospective analysis (ex post evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutionalize formal retrospective analysis of rules to determine whether regulations are delivering intended outcomes and at what cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies rarely conduct ex post estimates of benefits, costs, or efficacy. The primer recommends independent, predetermined-methodology reviews to assess both nonfunctional (obsolete/inefficient/ineffective) rules and cumulative effects of many rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze cumulative and off-budget effects of regulatory accumulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses should consider the cumulative effects of multiple regulations and off-budget compliance costs that do not appear in agency spending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory accumulation can have interactive effects, duplicative costs, and large off-budget burdens that dwarf on-budget agency spending. Prospective and retrospective analyses should account for these cumulative impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create an independent body or process for retrospective review
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an independent body (or provide authority to an existing independent organization) to analyze existing regulations with a predetermined methodology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retrospective review performed by the same agencies that created regulations is unlikely to be robust or candid; independence improves objectivity and the ability to identify obsolete or ineffective regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative impact accounting before enactment and as feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress should obtain impartial 'legislative impact accounting'—a comprehensive, objective assessment of the likely economic effects of legislation that authorizes regulation—before voting, and legislative impact accounting should be used as an ongoing feedback mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative impact accounting would be analogous to RIAs for agencies, could be overseen by CBO or another independent body, would help Congress use budgetary authority to correct regulatory programs, and would create a feedback loop transmitting results back to Congress to inform future action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link authorized spending/appropriations to expected regulatory outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Make authorized spending or appropriations for regulatory agencies linked to the outcomes Congress expects regulators to accomplish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under legislative impact accounting, agencies would manage regulatory and enforcement duties within account levels appropriated by Congress; if costs of new regulations exceed account limits, agencies would need to modify proposals or identify offsets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt 'one in, one out' regulatory offset policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Require agencies to eliminate one or more existing regulations for every new regulation proposed to curb regulatory accumulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executive Order 13771 implemented such a policy for executive branch agencies; the primer notes successes in jurisdictions like British Columbia and Canada and recommends an institutionalized, statutory approach to prevent repeal by future presidents and extend to independent agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure OIRA-like quality control applies to more regulations and agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend stringent analytical review (like OIRA review under EO 12866) or statutory equivalents to cover a larger share of regulations and to include independent agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executive orders currently cover only a small fraction of regulations (about 8%), and only 2% are subject to the most stringent tests; statutory requirements would close coverage gaps and raise analytical quality broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require agency analyses to address indirect and distributional effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses should consider indirect effects—e.g., job displacement in downstream industries—and distributional impacts, especially regressivity toward low- and middle-income households.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include EPA power rule impacts on associated industries and evidence that regulatory accumulation can act like a regressive sales tax or increase barriers to entry, harming entrepreneurship and income equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent agencies from avoiding procedural requirements (e.g., notice-and-comment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should be required to follow procedural rules (notice-and-comment, OIRA submission where applicable) and should not be allowed to systematically avoid these processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The primer documents that agencies avoided notice-and-comment for a large share of finalized regulations and recommends strengthening statutory process requirements so analysis informs decisions rather than serving post-hoc justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify and tighten the standard for judicial review of agency analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarify how courts should evaluate agency economic analyses under the Administrative Procedure Act so review is consistent and focused on significant analytical deficiencies rather than vague or inconsistent application of 'arbitrary and capricious'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifying RIA topics and evidentiary expectations in statute would help courts conduct consistent, substantive reviews and encourage better agency analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use best available evidence in regulatory impact analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Require agencies to base regulatory impact analyses on the best available evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress should require RIAs to rely on the best available empirical evidence; this reduces speculative or opinion-based claims and improves the credibility of projected benefits and costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus retrospective reviews on outcomes and efficacy, not merely paperwork savings
rubrics_metrics.description: Retrospective reviews should estimate ex post benefits, costs, and efficacy of rules rather than concentrate primarily on paperwork reduction or reporting streamlining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative reviews often emphasize paperwork or reporting savings; a proper retrospective analysis should evaluate whether economically important rules are delivering societal objectives cost-effectively.
